problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(6-6x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094290/assets/61388466bb2d97b5080707e769ae862e633bfb0fe1d2b5f16c75daa14da76e53.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(6-6x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=6-6x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6-6x & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=1\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  | $2$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $3>0$ | $0$ | $-6<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=1\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=6-6x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (6-6x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=6x-3{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-3{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{2})^{2} & =6(0)-3(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-3{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =12x-6{x}^{2}+8 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-6{x}^{2}+12x+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-6{x}^{2}+12x+8}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(1)=\sqrt{-6(1)^{2}+12(1)+8}=\sqrt{14}\,m/s
$$
